options: Osteoblast
Osteocyte
Osteogenic cell
Osteoclast

why.correct: The osteoclast is a very large cell with several nuclei and a frilled membrane pressed against the bone. It resorbs bone.
options: Osteoblasts are medium-sized cells with one nucleus that sit in rows on bone surfaces.
An osteocyte is a small cell with long branching arms, inside the matrix.
An osteogenic cell is a flat stem cell with one nucleus.
Correct. Huge, many nuclei, frilled edge on the bone: an osteoclast.

q: Name the pinned cells, which sit in a row on the bone surface.
options: Osteocytes
Osteoblasts
Osteoclasts
Chondrocytes

why.correct: Osteoblasts line up on bone surfaces and secrete osteoid, the organic matrix that later mineralizes.
options: Osteocytes sit alone inside the matrix, each in a lacuna, not in a row on the surface.
Correct. A row of bone-building cells on the surface is a row of osteoblasts.
Osteoclasts are single huge cells with many nuclei, not a row of ordinary-sized cells.
Chondrocytes are cartilage cells in lacunae within cartilage matrix, not bone-surface cells.

q: Name the pinned flat cell, the stem cell of bone.
options: Osteogenic cell
Osteoblast
Mesenchymal cell
Osteoclast

why.correct: The osteogenic cell is the stem cell of bone. It lies in the periosteum and endosteum, it is the only bone cell that divides, and its daughters become osteoblasts.
options: Correct. The dividing stem cell of bone is the osteogenic cell.
Osteoblasts are made from this cell, and they do not divide.
Mesenchymal cells are the embryonic cells that connective tissues come from. The pinned cell sits on a finished bone surface, as the stem cell of bone.
Osteoclasts come from a different line, related to macrophages, and they are huge, not flat.

q: Name the pinned struts of bone.
options: Osteons
Central canals
Trabeculae
Canaliculi

why.correct: Trabeculae are the thin struts of spongy bone, with marrow in the spaces between them.
options: Osteons are the cylinders of compact bone, each with a central canal. The struts of spongy bone have none.
Central canals are channels down the middle of osteons in compact bone. Spongy bone has none, and the pinned structures are solid struts.
Correct. The branching struts are trabeculae.
Canaliculi are hair-thin channels within the matrix, far smaller than the struts.

q: Name the pinned small cavity in the matrix.
options: Central canal
Lacuna
Perforating canal
Canaliculus

why.correct: A lacuna is a small cavity between lamellae. Each one holds a single osteocyte.
options: A central canal runs down the middle of an osteon and carries vessels. Spongy bone has none.
Correct. The small pit that holds an osteocyte is a lacuna.
A perforating canal is a channel running across compact bone between osteons, not a small cell-sized pit.
A canaliculus is a hair-thin channel running from a lacuna, not the cavity itself.

q: Name the pinned fine channels that run across the layers of matrix.
options: Canaliculi
Lacunae
Perforating canals
Collagen fibers

why.correct: Canaliculi are hair-thin channels that radiate from each lacuna. The arms of osteocytes run through them, linking the cells to each other and to a supply of blood.
options: Correct. The fine radiating channels are canaliculi.
Lacunae are the small cavities the channels connect, not the channels themselves.
Perforating canals are much larger channels in compact bone that carry vessels between osteons.
Collagen fibers are part of the matrix and are not visible as open channels.

q: A student soaks a chicken bone in vinegar for a week. It keeps its shape but bends like rubber. What did the vinegar remove?
options: The collagen and ground substance
The osteocytes
The calcium phosphate crystals
The periosteum

why.correct: Vinegar is an acid, and acid dissolves the calcium phosphate (hydroxyapatite) crystals, just as the acid from osteoclasts does. What remains is the collagen framework, which is flexible but cannot resist squeezing.
options: If the collagen and ground substance had gone, the bone would be hard and brittle, as it is after baking. The bone bends because they remain.
Removing cells would not change how hard or flexible the matrix is; the matrix sets those properties.
Correct. The acid dissolved the mineral and left the flexible collagen.
The periosteum is a thin outer membrane. Its loss would not make the whole bone rubbery.

q: Mia, 4, has had eleven broken bones. Her bones contain a normal amount of mineral, but a gene change makes her collagen faulty. Why do her bones break so easily?
options: Her bones cannot store calcium
Her bone lacks the flexibility to bend under a load
Her osteoclasts cannot resorb bone
Her bones have too few lacunae

why.correct: Collagen resists pulling and gives bone slight flexibility. Mineral without good collagen is like chalk: hard but brittle, so it snaps instead of bending. This inherited condition is called brittle bone disease.
options: The question says her bones hold a normal amount of mineral, so storage is not the problem.
Correct. Faulty collagen leaves hard but brittle bone.
Osteoclasts are not affected by a collagen defect, and failing to resorb bone would not in itself make bones snap.
Lacunae hold osteocytes. A collagen defect does not remove them, and it is the matrix that sets strength.

q: Which bone cell is the only one that divides?
options: Osteoblast
Mature osteocyte
Osteoclast
Osteogenic cell

why.correct: Osteogenic cells are the stem cells of bone. They divide, and their daughters differentiate into osteoblasts.
options: Osteoblasts are made by osteogenic cells and do not divide.
Osteocytes are former osteoblasts trapped in matrix; they do not divide.
Osteoclasts form by fusion of precursor cells, not by division, and do not divide.
Correct. Only the osteogenic cell divides.
Osteoblasts that change their job
Fused precursor cells of the macrophage line
Osteocytes released from their lacunae
Osteogenic cells of the periosteum

why.correct: Osteoclasts form when several precursor cells from the blood-forming line in red marrow, the line that also makes macrophages, fuse. That is why they have several nuclei. They are not part of the osteogenic cell to osteoblast to osteocyte line.
options: Osteoblasts become osteocytes, not osteoclasts. The two cell types come from different lines.
Correct. Osteoclasts are fused cells of the macrophage line.
Osteocytes stay in their lacunae for life. They do not become osteoclasts.
Osteogenic cells make osteoblasts. Osteoclasts come from a separate, blood-forming line.

q: Put the steps in order to show how a new osteocyte comes to be.
options: An osteogenic cell in the periosteum divides
A daughter cell differentiates into an osteoblast
The osteoblast secretes osteoid around itself
Calcium phosphate crystals deposit in the osteoid
The cell is walled into a lacuna and becomes an osteocyte, keeping contact through canaliculi

why.correct: Osteogenic cells divide and their daughters become osteoblasts. An osteoblast secretes osteoid, which then mineralizes. As matrix builds up around it, the cell ends up enclosed in a lacuna. It is now an osteocyte, still linked to its neighbors by arms running through canaliculi.

q: In an experiment, the canaliculi around a group of osteocytes in compact bone are blocked. What happens to those osteocytes?
options: They carry on normally
They divide to make new canaliculi
They turn into osteoclasts
They die, cut off from oxygen and nutrients

why.correct: Mineralized matrix is almost impermeable. Osteocytes get oxygen and nutrients only from vessels in the central canal, passed along through canaliculi. Block the canaliculi and the cells starve.
options: They cannot carry on normally: nutrients cannot diffuse through mineralized matrix, which is why canaliculi exist.
Osteocytes do not divide.
Osteocytes do not become osteoclasts; the two come from different cell lines.
Correct. The canaliculi are their only supply line.

q: Select every feature of spongy bone.
options: Built of trabeculae
Organized into osteons with central canals
Spaces that can hold red marrow
Fills the ends of long bones
Makes up about 80% of the skeleton's mass
Osteocytes in lacunae

why.correct: Spongy bone is a lattice of trabeculae with marrow in the spaces between them. It fills the ends of long bones and the inside of other bones, and its osteocytes sit in lacunae like those of compact bone.
options: Correct. Trabeculae are its struts.
Osteons with central canals are the units of compact bone. Trabeculae are thin enough not to need a central canal.
Correct. Its spaces hold marrow, red in some bones.
Correct. The epiphyses are filled with spongy bone.
About 80% of the skeleton's mass is compact bone. Spongy bone is about 20%.
Correct. Osteocytes of spongy bone also live in lacunae, linked by canaliculi.

q: Complete the bone cell line: osteogenic cell → ____ → osteocyte.
options: Osteoclast
Chondrocyte
Osteoblast
Fibroblast

why.correct: Osteogenic cells become osteoblasts, and osteoblasts walled in by their own matrix become osteocytes.
options: Osteoclasts come from a different line, related to macrophages, and do not become osteocytes.
Chondrocytes are cartilage cells, not a stage between bone stem cells and osteocytes.
Correct. The osteoblast is the middle stage.
Fibroblasts make connective tissue fibers and are not part of the bone cell line.

q: A student describes how an osteoclast resorbs bone. One step is wrong. Which one?
options: The osteoclast seals its frilled membrane onto the bone surface
It pumps hydrogen ions onto the bone
The acid dissolves the calcium phosphate crystals
Enzymes from its lysosomes digest the collagen
The released calcium and phosphate are locked away inside the osteoclast

why.correct: The calcium and phosphate freed from the matrix move into the blood. That is how bone works as a mineral bank: osteoclasts withdraw minerals from it.
options: This step is right. The sealed space keeps the acid and enzymes against the bone.
This step is right. Pumped hydrogen ions acidify the sealed space.
This step is right. Acid dissolves hydroxyapatite.
This step is right. Once the mineral is gone, lysosomal enzymes digest the exposed collagen.
This is the error. The released minerals pass into the blood rather than being stored in the cell.
The spongy bone between the two plates of a flat skull bone
The outer shell of compact bone that covers every bone of the skeleton
The lining membrane of the medullary cavity
The central canal of an osteon

why.correct: In the flat bones of the skull, a layer of spongy bone is sandwiched between two plates of compact bone. That spongy layer is the diploë.
options: Correct. Diploë is the name for spongy bone in flat skull bones.
The outer shell is compact bone; the diploë is the spongy layer inside it.
The lining of the medullary cavity is the endosteum.
The central canal is the vessel channel of an osteon, found in compact bone.

q: Which channels run at right angles to the central canals and connect neighboring osteons with each other and with the periosteum?
options: Canaliculi
Central (Haversian) canals
Perforating canals
Trabeculae

why.correct: Perforating canals run across compact bone, crosswise to the osteons. They carry vessels between central canals and out to the periosteum and marrow.
options: Canaliculi are tiny channels that link lacunae to each other and to the central canal within one osteon. They are too small to carry blood vessels.
Central canals run along the length of each osteon. The channels asked about run across the bone, joining those central canals.
Correct. Perforating canals connect the central canals crosswise.
Trabeculae are the struts of spongy bone, not channels in compact bone.

q: In one lamella of an osteon, the collagen fibers spiral one way; in the next lamella, they spiral the opposite way. What does this arrangement help the osteon resist?
options: Being dissolved by acid
Twisting forces
Blood vessel growth
Mineral deposition

why.correct: Like the crossed layers of plywood, fibers that spiral in opposite directions in neighboring lamellae resist twisting from either direction.
options: Acid dissolves mineral whatever direction the collagen runs.
Correct. Alternating fiber directions resist twisting.
Vessels run in the central and perforating canals; fiber direction does not block them.
Mineral deposits along the collagen fibers in every lamella; their direction does not prevent it.

q: When an adult's bone is being lost, the spongy bone of the vertebrae thins faster than the compact bone of the limb shafts. Which property of spongy bone best explains this?
options: It has no osteocytes
It contains no collagen
It has no blood supply
Its large surface gives bone cells more room to work

why.correct: Osteoblasts and osteoclasts work on bone surfaces. The thin trabeculae of spongy bone expose far more surface per gram than compact bone does, so a shift toward breakdown removes spongy bone faster.
options: Spongy bone has osteocytes in lacunae, just as compact bone does.
Spongy bone has the same matrix of collagen and mineral as compact bone.
Spongy bone is well supplied by the vessels of the marrow between its trabeculae.
Correct. More surface means faster turnover in either direction.
